train.content: What's the difference between backend and frontend?

Frontend is what the user sees and interacts with — the website design, buttons, forms, animations. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and frameworks like React, Vue. Backend is the server side running behind the scenes — database operations, user authentication, business logic. Built with Python (Django, Flask), Node.js, Java (Spring). Someone who does both is called a full-stack developer. Gorkem is active on the full-stack side — React/React Native for frontend and Python for backend. If you're starting out, learn frontend first — seeing visual results boosts motivation.

train.content: What does async/await mean?

Async/await is a pattern for asynchronous programming. In synchronous programming operations run sequentially — one must finish before the next starts. In async, multiple operations can progress in parallel. Say you're making 3 API calls — synchronously it takes 9 seconds (3 each), asynchronously they all run in parallel and finish in 3 seconds. Python uses asyncio, JavaScript uses Promises and async/await. Used heavily in web apps, API calls, file operations. Critical for performance — especially I/O-bound operations.

train.content: What does a web framework do?

A web framework handles the repetitive code you'd write when building web applications. Routing, database connections, user authentication, form handling — all provided out of the box. In Python, Django (full-featured, big projects) and Flask (minimal, small projects) are most popular. JavaScript has Express.js, Ruby has Rails, PHP has Laravel. Without a framework you'd write everything from scratch which is a huge time sink. But understanding what's under the framework matters — knowing just the framework isn't enough, understand HTTP and the request-response cycle.

train.content: How does AI image generation work?

Image generation now uses diffusion models — Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, Midjourney are the most popular examples. The concept: you give the model random noise and it gradually denoises to create the desired image. For text-to-image, the text is first converted to an embedding which guides the diffusion process. GANs are still used but diffusion models surpassed them in quality. Gorkem's computer vision projects are on the analysis side but image generation uses the same foundations.

train.content: Why use virtual environments?

Virtual environments isolate project dependencies in Python. Say one project uses Django 4.0 and another uses Django 3.2. Both on the same machine but need different versions. Without virtual environments one overwrites the other. Create one with python3 -m venv myenv, activate with source myenv/bin/activate. Using a separate venv per project is best practice. pip freeze > requirements.txt saves dependencies, someone else runs pip install -r requirements.txt to get the same setup.

train.content: How do I manage my time?

The foundation of time management is prioritization. Use the Eisenhower matrix: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, neither. Most people spend too much time on urgent but unimportant tasks. Every evening write tomorrow's to-do list — maximum 3-5 items. Pomodoro technique really works: 25 minutes focus, 5 minutes break. Don't multitask — one thing at a time. Try time blocking — assign specific hours to specific tasks in your calendar. Put your phone on silent while working.

train.content: Why is exception handling important?

Exception handling prevents your program from crashing on unexpected situations. Python uses try-except blocks. Reading a file that doesn't exist — FileNotFoundError. Making an API request with no internet — ConnectionError. User enters text instead of a number — ValueError. If you don't catch these, the program crashes and the user has a bad experience. But don't put try-except everywhere — only catch errors that can actually occur. Catching general Exception is bad practice because it hides real bugs.

train.content: What is list comprehension in Python?

List comprehension is a concise way to create lists in Python. For example [x**2 for x in range(10)] gives you squares from 0 to 9. What would take 3-4 lines with a regular for loop, you do in 1 line. You can add conditions too: [x for x in range(100) if x % 2 == 0] gives even numbers. Great for readability but don't make them too complex or they become unreadable. Keep it simple. Gorkem's Python projects probably use them extensively.

train.content: Why is quantum computing different from regular computers?

Regular computers use bits — 0 or 1. Quantum computers use qubits — 0, 1, or both simultaneously (superposition). There's also entanglement — two qubits linked so one's state affects the other. These properties mean some problems (cryptography, molecule simulation, optimization) that would take years on regular computers could take seconds on quantum computers. But it's still very early — qubits are fragile, error rates are high, they don't work at room temperature. IBM, Google, Microsoft are investing heavily. We might see practical applications in 5-10 years.

train.content: What is recursion?

Recursion is when a function calls itself. Classic example: factorial calculation. 5! = 5 x 4! and 4! = 4 x 3! continuing down until 1! = 1 which stops it. Every recursion needs two things: base case (stopping condition) and recursive case (calling itself). Without a base case you get infinite recursion and a stack overflow error. Fibonacci sequence, tree traversal, QuickSort algorithm all use recursion. Some problems are much more elegant to solve with recursion, but performance-wise iterative solutions can sometimes be better.
